name: Economics Basics
author: Recurse
subject: humanities
description: Scarcity, supply and demand, market failures, GDP, inflation, recessions and policy, trade, and compound interest.

lesson.intro: Economics studies how people, firms and governments choose when resources are limited. Its core ideas explain everyday things: why prices jump after a bad harvest, why central banks change interest rates, and why countries trade.
objectives: Identify opportunity costs and sunk costs in everyday decisions
Predict how supply and demand shifts change price and quantity, and use elasticity
Recognize market structures and failures such as externalities and public goods
Explain GDP, inflation, unemployment, and the policy response to a downturn
Use comparative advantage and compound interest to reason about trade and saving

sections.title: Scarcity and opportunity cost
sections.key: Every choice has an opportunity cost, the value of the next best alternative you give up, while sunk costs are already gone and should not sway decisions.
sections.body:
Economics starts from **scarcity**: time, money, land, labor and materials are limited, but wants are not. So every person, firm and government has to choose.

The **opportunity cost** of a choice is only the best option you passed over, not the sum of every alternative:

[[visual]]

**Sunk costs** are already paid and cannot be recovered. They are the same whatever you choose next, so they should not affect the decision. Sticking with something only because you already paid for it is the **sunk cost fallacy**.

Economists also think **at the margin**: compare the extra benefit of one more unit (one more hour, one more worker) with its extra cost.

visual.title: Opportunity costs
rows: Studying for an evening instead of a $60 paid shift
$60, even though no money changes hands
Tuition plus the wages you could have earned
Less for health or schools, unless it taxes or borrows more

sections.pitfall: Letting sunk costs drive decisions. Money already spent and unrecoverable is the same whatever you choose next, so only future costs and benefits count.

check.question: A city spends $10 million building a stadium. What is the opportunity cost of that decision?
choices: Zero, as long as the stadium later earns back its cost
The $10 million plus every other project the city could fund
The most valuable alternative use of the money, such as a new school
Only the interest the city could have earned on $10 million
check.explanation: Opportunity cost is the single best alternative given up, not every alternative added together. Earning money back later does not erase what the city could have done with the money now.

sections.title: Supply, demand and elasticity
sections.key: Prices settle where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded; a change in anything but the good's own price shifts a whole curve and moves that equilibrium.
sections.body:
In a market, buyers and sellers together set prices.

- **Law of demand**: when the price rises, people buy less, other things equal.
- **Law of supply**: when the price rises, producers offer more, because selling pays better.

[[visual]]

A change in the good's own price moves you **along** its curve. Anything else **shifts** the whole curve:

- Demand shifts with income, tastes, expectations, and the prices of substitutes and complements.
- Supply shifts with input costs, technology, weather and the number of sellers.

[[visual 2]]

**Price elasticity of demand** is the % change in quantity demanded divided by the % change in price, written as a positive number. Above 1, demand is **elastic**; below 1, **inelastic**.

[[visual 3]]

[[visual 4]]

visual.title: Equilibrium
rows: Surplus: unsold goods push the price down. A price floor set above it, such as a minimum milk price, keeps a surplus
Shortage: buyers compete and push the price up. A price ceiling set below it, such as strict rent control, causes shortages

visual.title: What a shift does
visual.caption: A drought cuts the wheat harvest: supply falls, so the price rises and less is sold.

steps.label: % change in quantity / % change in price

items.title: Inelastic
points: Necessities with few substitutes, such as insulin
Buyers barely cut back when the price rises
Raising the price raises total revenue

items.title: Elastic
points: Goods with many close substitutes, such as one brand of cereal
Buyers switch away when the price rises
Raising the price lowers total revenue

sections.pitfall: Confusing a shift with a movement along a curve. The good's own price moves along the curve; anything else that changes how much people want or offer at every price shifts it.

check.question: A rainy season makes more people want umbrellas at every price. What happens to the equilibrium?
choices: The price falls and fewer umbrellas are sold
The price rises and more umbrellas are sold
The price rises and fewer umbrellas are sold
Nothing changes until suppliers decide to react
check.explanation: Demand shifts right. At the old price there is a shortage, so the price rises, and sellers respond by offering more, so both price and quantity rise.

sections.title: Market structures and market failures
sections.key: The fewer the sellers, the more they can charge, and even competitive markets fail with externalities and public goods.
sections.body:
How much power sellers have depends on the **market structure**:

[[visual]]

The less competition, the more firms can charge. Compared with a competitive market, a monopoly typically charges a higher price and sells less.

Markets can fail even when firms compete. An **externality** is a cost or benefit that falls on people outside the deal:

[[visual 2]]

A **public good** is **non-excludable** (people who do not pay cannot be stopped from using it) and **non-rival** (one person's use does not reduce what others get). Street lighting and national defense are examples. People can **free-ride**, so private firms cannot charge enough to provide them, and governments usually fund them through taxes.

visual.title: Market structures
rows: None: each firm is a price taker
A few large firms that watch and react to each other
One, protected by barriers to entry

items.title: Negative externality
points: The price leaves out the harm to others
Fix: taxes, regulation or tradable permits

sections.pitfall: Assuming a market with many sellers always gets things right. Pollution and public goods show markets can fail even when competition is fierce.

check.question: Compared with a competitive market, what does a monopoly typically do?
choices: Charge a lower price to attract more buyers
Sell a larger quantity at the same price
Charge the same price but offer better quality
Charge a higher price and sell a smaller quantity
check.explanation: With no rivals to undercut it, a monopoly can restrict output and raise its price above the competitive level. Some buyers who would have paid the competitive price go without.

sections.title: GDP, inflation and central banks
sections.key: GDP measures output and inflation measures rising prices; central banks raise interest rates to cool inflation and cut them to support a weak economy.
sections.body:
**Gross domestic product** (GDP) is the market value of all final goods and services a country produces in a period. "Final" avoids double counting: flour sold to a bakery counts only inside the bread's price. Resold used goods and unpaid work at home are left out.

[[visual]]

**Inflation** is a sustained rise in the general price level, usually measured with a consumer price index. At 3% a year, $100 buys about 3% less a year later. Unexpected inflation hurts savers and fixed incomes, and helps borrowers with fixed-rate debt. The **real interest rate** is roughly the nominal rate minus inflation.

**Central banks** aim for low, stable inflation, often about 2% a year. Their main tool is a short-term policy interest rate:

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Reading GDP
rows: Consumption + investment + government purchases + exports - imports
Output at current prices: it can rise from inflation alone
Adjusted for inflation: it rises only when output grows
A rough guide to average living standards

visual.title: When the central bank raises rates

steps.label: The central bank raises its policy rate
Banks raise the rates on loans and mortgages
Households and firms borrow and spend less
Demand for goods and services cools
Inflation eases
steps.detail: at the risk of slower growth and higher unemployment

visual.caption: Cutting rates works the other way, encouraging borrowing and spending in a downturn.

sections.deeper: Examples of central banks: the US Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of England. Most are independent of day-to-day politics, so that they can raise rates when it is unpopular.
sections.pitfall: Comparing GDP across years without adjusting for prices. Nominal GDP can rise purely because of inflation; use real GDP to see whether output actually grew.

check.question: What does real GDP adjust for that nominal GDP does not?
choices: Changes in the general price level
Growth in the size of the population
The value of imports and exports
Unpaid work done in the home
check.explanation: Real GDP values output at constant prices, so it rises only if the economy produces more, not just because prices went up. Adjusting for population gives GDP per person, a different measure.

sections.title: Recessions, unemployment and fiscal policy
sections.key: Economies cycle through expansions and recessions; the unemployed are people actively looking for work, and governments respond with monetary and fiscal policy.
sections.body:
In late 2009 US unemployment reached 10%, and in April 2020, as lockdowns began, it briefly hit about 15%. Output rises and falls in the **business cycle**: expansion, peak, contraction, trough. A **recession** is a significant, broad decline in activity; a rule of thumb is two quarters in a row of falling real GDP.

**Unemployed** means no job, available, and actively looking. Retirees, full-time students and people who gave up looking are outside the labor force.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

Some support is automatic: tax revenue falls and benefits rise as people lose jobs. These are **automatic stabilizers**. Spending more than tax revenue in a year is a budget **deficit**, and the total of past borrowing is the national **debt**. Deficits in recessions are normal; large ones in good times keep pushing the debt up.

visual.title: Three kinds of unemployment
rows: Between jobs or entering the workforce; some is normal and healthy
Someone who quit to look for a better job
Workers' skills or locations do not match the jobs available
Automation or imports close down an industry
A recession: firms sell less and cut staff
Layoffs across many firms in a downturn

visual.title: Two sets of tools
rows: Cut taxes or raise spending, on roads or unemployment benefits

sections.pitfall: Counting everyone without a job as unemployed. Retirees, full-time students and people who have stopped looking are outside the labor force, not unemployed.

check.question: A country has 95 million employed people and 5 million unemployed people looking for work. What is its unemployment rate?
check.explanation: The labor force is 95 + 5 = 100 million, and 5 / 100 = 5%. Dividing by the employed only (5 / 95 ≈ 5.3%) leaves the unemployed out of the labor force, which is the usual slip.

sections.title: Comparative advantage and trade
sections.key: Trade follows comparative advantage, the lower opportunity cost, so both sides gain even when one is better at making everything.
sections.body:
A producer has an **absolute advantage** in a good if it can make more of it with the same resources. It has a **comparative advantage** if it makes the good at a lower **opportunity cost**. Trade follows comparative advantage, an idea set out by David Ricardo in 1817.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

If Lena fishes, Omar picks coconuts, and they trade at a rate between their costs, say 3 coconuts per fish, both end up with more than they could produce alone.

Countries work the same way: specializing and trading raises total output and lowers prices. The gains are uneven, though: workers and firms that compete with imports can lose out.

A **tariff** is a tax on imports. It raises prices for domestic buyers, protects some domestic producers and usually shrinks the total gains from trade. Targeted countries often retaliate.

visual.title: What each can make in one day
visual.caption: Lena is better at both: she has the absolute advantage in each.

visual.title: Who has the comparative advantage?
visual.result: Lena should fish and Omar should pick coconuts: each gives up less

sections.pitfall: Thinking the more productive country gains nothing from trade. Comparative advantage is about opportunity cost, and every country has a lowest-cost option.

check.question: What is a tariff?
choices: A limit on how many goods a country may export
A subsidy paid to firms that sell abroad
An agreement to remove barriers to trade
A tax on goods imported from abroad
check.explanation: A tariff taxes imports, raising their price for domestic buyers. It can protect domestic producers that compete with imports, but consumers pay more and the total gains from trade usually shrink.

sections.title: Money, banks and compound interest
sections.key: Compound interest earns interest on earlier interest, so money grows faster and faster; by the rule of 72 it doubles in about 72 / rate years.
sections.body:
Why does a savings account pay interest, and why can a forgotten credit card balance spiral? Money, banks and compounding explain both.

[[visual]]

**Banks** take deposits and lend most of them out, earning the gap between the rates they charge and pay. They keep only a small fraction as cash, so a **bank run**, too many withdrawals at once, can sink one. **Deposit insurance** stops the panic: the US FDIC covers up to $250,000 per depositor at each insured bank.

**Compound interest** is interest on earlier interest: after n years at 5%, $1,000 becomes $1,000 × 1.05ⁿ.

[[visual 2]]

**Rule of 72**: money doubles in about 72 / rate years, so about 12 years at 6%. On debt it works against you: a credit card balance at 24% roughly doubles in 3 years. Save early: the first dollars compound longest.

visual.title: Money's three jobs
rows: You can buy things with it
It keeps buying power over time, though inflation chips away at it
visual.caption: Most modern money is not cash but bank deposits.

visual.title: $1,000 at 5% a year
visual.caption: Simple interest pays only on the original $1,000. Compound interest pays on the growing balance.

sections.deeper:
**Banks create money.** When a bank makes a loan, it credits the borrower's account, so new deposits, and new money, appear.

**Stocks and bonds.** Stocks are shares of ownership in companies; bonds are loans to governments or companies. Over long periods stocks have historically returned more than bonds, but with much bigger swings along the way.

**Diversification**, spreading money across many investments, reduces the risk that one failure wipes you out.
sections.pitfall: Treating compound growth as simple growth. At 5% a year for 30 years your money grows more than fourfold, not 2.5 times, because each year's interest earns interest too.

check.question: Using the rule of 72, about how long does money take to double at 8% a year?
choices: 8 years
9 years
12.5 years
72 years
check.explanation: 72 / 8 = 9 years. Check: 1.08⁹ ≈ 2.0. 12.5 years is what simple interest gives (8% × 12.5 = 100%), which ignores interest on interest.

keyTerms.definition: The value of the next best alternative given up when making a choice.
The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
The percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.
A cost or benefit of an activity that falls on people outside the transaction.
A good that is non-excludable and non-rival, such as street lighting or national defense.
The market value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a given period.
A sustained rise in the general price level, which reduces what money can buy.
The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than someone else.
A significant, broad decline in economic activity; a common rule of thumb is two quarters in a row of falling real GDP.
The government's use of spending and taxes to influence the economy, as opposed to the central bank's monetary policy.
Interest earned on both the original amount and the interest already added, so savings and debts grow exponentially.

summary: Every choice has an opportunity cost; sunk costs should not affect decisions.
Prices settle where supply meets demand, and shifts in either move that point.
Less competition means higher prices; markets overproduce harms and underprovide public goods.
Central banks move interest rates and governments adjust taxes and spending to steady the cycle.
Trading by comparative advantage lets both sides consume more.
Compound interest multiplies money over time; the rule of 72 estimates doubling time.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why a country that is better at making everything can still gain by trading with a country that is worse at making everything.

questions.question: Maya could work a Saturday shift that pays $90, or go to a free concert. She goes to the concert. What is her opportunity cost?
choices: Nothing, because the concert was free
The $90 she could have earned
The price other people paid for tickets
Only her time, but not any money
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up. By choosing the concert Maya gave up $90 in wages, even though she paid nothing at the door. "Free" activities still cost the alternatives you pass up.

questions.question: What term means the value of the next best alternative you give up when you make a choice?
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost counts only the best option you passed over, not every possible alternative. It applies to time as well as money.

questions.question: You paid $50 for a non-refundable concert ticket, but on the day you feel unwell and would rather stay home. How should the $50 affect your decision?
choices: You should go, or else the $50 will be wasted
You should go if the ticket cost more than a usual night out
You should stay home so that you save the $50
It should not matter, because the $50 is a sunk cost
questions.explanation: The $50 is gone whichever you choose, so it should not affect the decision. Compare only what lies ahead: the enjoyment of going against the effort of going while unwell. Going "so the ticket isn't wasted" is the sunk cost fallacy, and staying home does not get the money back either.

questions.question: A frost destroys much of Florida's orange crop. What happens in the market for oranges?
choices: Supply falls, so the price rises and fewer oranges are sold
Demand falls, so the price falls and fewer oranges are sold
Supply falls, so the price falls and more oranges are sold
Demand rises, so the price and quantity both rise
questions.explanation: The frost reduces how much growers can offer at every price, shifting supply to the left. At the old price there is a shortage, so the price rises until buyers cut back. Buyers' tastes have not changed, so demand has not shifted.

questions.question: A government sets a minimum price for milk above the equilibrium price. What results?
choices: A shortage, because buyers want more than sellers offer
No change, because the market price was already lower
A surplus, because sellers offer more than buyers want
A rise in demand until buyers accept the higher price
questions.explanation: At a price above equilibrium, farmers supply more milk and buyers purchase less, leaving unsold milk, a surplus. A price held below equilibrium does the opposite and creates a shortage.

questions.question: Which change shifts the demand curve for coffee, rather than moving along it?
choices: The price of coffee falls, so people buy more of it
A health study makes people want more coffee at any price
Coffee growers bring in a record harvest this year
The price of coffee rises, so people buy less of it
questions.explanation: A change in tastes changes how much people want at every price, so the whole demand curve shifts right. A change in coffee's own price only moves along the curve, and a bigger harvest shifts supply, not demand.

questions.question: The price of a snack rises by 10% and the quantity demanded falls by 5%. What is the price elasticity of demand, written as a positive number?
questions.explanation: Elasticity = % change in quantity demanded / % change in price = 5 / 10 = 0.5. Because it is below 1, demand for the snack is inelastic: buyers react only weakly to the price change.

questions.question: Demand for a product is price inelastic. If the seller raises the price, what happens to total revenue?
choices: It falls, because any price rise drives some buyers away
It stays the same, because price and quantity changes cancel out
It rises, because quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises
It falls, because buyers switch to substitutes in large numbers
questions.explanation: Revenue is price times quantity. With inelastic demand, for example a 10% price rise and a 4% fall in sales, the price effect wins and revenue rises. Mass switching to substitutes describes elastic demand, where a price rise would cut revenue.

questions.question: Which market is the closest example of an oligopoly?
choices: A mobile phone network market dominated by three or four big providers
Wheat farming, with thousands of farms selling identical grain
Restaurants in a large city, each with its own menu
A single water company that serves an entire town
questions.explanation: An oligopoly has a few large firms that watch and react to one another, like mobile networks or airlines. Wheat farming is close to perfect competition, city restaurants are monopolistic competition, and a sole water company is a monopoly.

questions.question: What market structure has a single seller and barriers to entry that keep rivals out?
questions.explanation: A monopoly faces no direct competition, so it can charge more and sell less than a competitive market would. Barriers include patents, control of a key resource, or very high setup costs, as with a water network.

questions.question: A factory's smoke harms people living nearby, and they receive no compensation. What is this, and what tends to happen?
choices: A positive externality, so too little is produced
A public good, so the government must provide it
A monopoly, so the price is set too high
A negative externality, so the product is overproduced
questions.explanation: The harm falls on third parties and is left out of the product's price, so the price is too low and more is produced than is good for society. A pollution tax, regulation or tradable permits can make the producer take the harm into account.

questions.question: Explain why private markets tend to underprovide public goods such as street lighting.
questions.answer: Public goods are non-excludable and non-rival: once the lights are on, everyone benefits whether or not they paid, and one person's use does not reduce anyone else's. People can free-ride, so a private seller cannot collect enough payment, which is why governments usually fund public goods through taxes.
questions.explanation: Markets work when sellers can charge each user. When non-payers cannot be excluded, too few people pay voluntarily and the good is underprovided or not provided at all.

questions.question: Which of these is counted in this year's GDP?
choices: A new bicycle made and sold this year
A used car resold this year
Flour bought by a bakery to make bread
A parent cooking dinner at home
questions.explanation: GDP counts the market value of final goods and services produced this period. The used car was counted when it was new, the flour is counted inside the price of the bread, and unpaid work at home is not counted.

questions.question: A savings account pays 5% interest a year and inflation is 3%. What is the approximate real interest rate, in percent?
questions.explanation: The real interest rate is roughly the nominal rate minus inflation: 5% - 3% = 2%. Your balance grows 5%, but prices rise 3%, so what your money can buy grows only about 2%.

questions.question: A central bank raises its policy interest rate. What is the usual intended effect?
choices: Borrowing becomes cheaper, so spending and inflation rise
Borrowing becomes costlier, so spending slows and inflation eases
The government must cut taxes by the same amount
Prices of all goods are frozen at their current level
questions.explanation: Higher policy rates feed through to loans and mortgages. People and firms borrow and spend less and save more, which cools demand and brings inflation down, at the risk of slower growth. Cutting rates has the opposite effect.

questions.question: In one day Ana can bake 10 loaves or sew 5 shirts. Ben can bake 4 loaves or sew 4 shirts. Who has the comparative advantage in shirts?
choices: Ana, because she can sew more shirts per day than Ben
Neither, because Ana is more productive at both goods
Ben, because each shirt costs him 1 loaf versus 2 loaves for Ana
Ana, because each shirt costs her fewer loaves than it costs Ben
questions.explanation: For Ana, 5 shirts cost 10 loaves, so 1 shirt costs 2 loaves. For Ben, 4 shirts cost 4 loaves, so 1 shirt costs 1 loaf. Ben gives up less to make a shirt, so he has the comparative advantage in shirts, even though Ana has the absolute advantage in both goods.

questions.question: Explain why two countries can both gain from trade even if one of them is more productive at making everything.
questions.answer: What matters is opportunity cost, not absolute productivity. If each country specializes in the good it gives up the least to make (its comparative advantage) and trades for the rest, total output rises and both can consume more than they could alone.
questions.explanation: Even a less productive country has a lower opportunity cost in something. Specializing on that basis means the world gets more of both goods from the same resources, and trade shares the gain.

questions.question: Match each market to its structure.
questions.explanation: Identical products from many sellers is perfect competition; many sellers with slightly different products is monopolistic competition; a few big rivals is oligopoly; one seller behind barriers is monopoly.

questions.question: Match each situation to the type of unemployment.

pairs.left: A graduate searching for a first job
Coal miners laid off as mines close for good
Factory workers laid off when sales collapse in a recession

questions.explanation: Frictional unemployment is the normal time spent finding a match. Structural unemployment comes from a lasting mismatch, here a shrinking industry. Cyclical unemployment rises and falls with the business cycle.

questions.question: Using the rule of 72, about how many years does money take to double at 4% interest a year?
questions.explanation: 72 / 4 = 18 years. The rule of 72 is a quick estimate of compound growth; at 4% the exact answer is about 17.7 years.

questions.question: You deposit $2,000 at 10% interest, compounded once a year. How much is in the account after 2 years, in dollars?
questions.explanation: After year 1: 2,000 × 1.10 = 2,200. After year 2: 2,200 × 1.10 = 2,420. Simple interest would give 2,400; the extra $20 is interest earned on the first year's interest.

questions.question: Which is an example of fiscal policy?
choices: The central bank cuts its policy interest rate
The government cuts income taxes to boost spending
A commercial bank raises its mortgage rates
The central bank sets an inflation target of 2%
questions.explanation: Fiscal policy is the government's taxing and spending. Interest rates and inflation targets are monetary policy, run by the central bank, and a commercial bank's own rates are a business decision.

questions.question: A country's labor force is 50 million people, and 3 million of them are unemployed. What is the unemployment rate, in percent?
questions.explanation: Unemployment rate = unemployed / labor force × 100 = 3 / 50 × 100 = 6%. The labor force already includes the unemployed, so there is nothing to add.

questions.question: Select every change that would shift the demand curve for electric cars to the right.
choices: Gasoline prices rise sharply
Consumers' incomes rise
The government gives buyers a tax credit for each electric car
The price of electric cars falls
Battery costs fall for car makers
questions.explanation: Pricier gasoline makes gasoline cars, the substitute, less attractive; higher incomes raise demand for a normal good; and a buyer's credit makes people want more at every sticker price. A fall in the car's own price is a movement along the curve, and cheaper batteries shift supply, not demand.

questions.question: Inflation turns out much higher than anyone expected. Who is most likely to benefit?
choices: A retiree living on a fixed pension
A saver holding cash
A lender who made fixed-rate loans
A homeowner with a fixed-rate mortgage
questions.explanation: The homeowner repays a fixed amount with money that is worth less, so the real burden of the debt shrinks. The lender is on the other side of that deal and loses, and fixed incomes and cash both buy less.

questions.question: Every price in a shop is written in dollars. Which function of money does this show?
choices: Medium of exchange
Store of value
Unit of account
Source of interest
questions.explanation: Measuring and comparing values in a common unit is money's role as a unit of account. Paying with it is the medium of exchange, and keeping it for later is the store of value.

questions.question: Put the effects of a central bank interest rate rise in order.
items: The central bank raises its policy rate
Banks raise the rates on loans and mortgages
Households and firms borrow and spend less
Demand for goods and services cools
questions.explanation: Monetary policy works through borrowing costs. The effects take time, often a year or more, which is why central banks act on forecasts rather than waiting for inflation to fall on its own.

questions.question: With all its resources, country X can make 20 tons of steel or 40 tons of wheat. Country Y can make 10 tons of steel or 30 tons of wheat. Which country should specialize in steel?
choices: Y, because it is worse at steel overall
Neither, because X is better at making both goods
Y, because steel costs it fewer tons of wheat
X, because a ton of steel costs it 2 tons of wheat versus 3 for Y
questions.explanation: For X, 20 steel trade off against 40 wheat, so 1 steel costs 2 wheat. For Y, 10 steel cost 30 wheat, so 1 steel costs 3 wheat. X gives up less, so it has the comparative advantage in steel, and Y in wheat.

questions.question: Why do governments insure bank deposits, as the FDIC does in the United States?
choices: To guarantee that every bank makes a profit
To stop bank runs, since banks keep only a fraction of deposits as cash
Because banks must keep every deposit in their vaults
To set the inflation rate directly
questions.explanation: Banks lend out most deposits, so they cannot repay everyone at once. If depositors know their money is insured, they have no reason to rush to withdraw it, which prevents the panic that could sink a healthy bank.
